finalAnswer:
I couldn't find anything showing what Congress said about EPA's budget this week (about Oct 2–8, 2026). I ran one general web search, and nothing it returned covers that week's floor remarks, hearings, or statements. The results were:

- **Senate EPW Committee hearings page:** The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee held its hearing on EPA's proposed FY2027 budget on **April 29, 2026**. Its listed hearings since then are on other topics: a Fish and Wildlife Service budget hearing in June, a nuclear waste policy hearing on Sept 23, and business meetings. None are on EPA's budget this week. The page doesn't include what was said at the April hearing.
- **EPA's testimony page:** It lists only 2025 testimony, including Administrator Zeldin's May 2025 FY2026 budget hearings. It hasn't been updated for this session, so it's no help for this week.
- **A snippet from an Oct 2 article on a Senate permitting reform bill:** It says the administration's proposed EPA budget "sought an additional $14 million to 'cut through the red tape,' despite slashing the agency's overall budget." That's a description of the proposal, not a congressional statement from this week.
- **Two items from Oct 8 that aren't about EPA's budget:** One is a Congressional Research Service report on PFAS remediation, dated Oct 7. The other is a PEER press release urging Congress to use a budget bill to block data centers on public lands.

I can try again with narrower sources if you'd like:
- The Congressional Record and committee hearings through the GovInfo Actor. It needs a free API key to be reliable, and it returns document links rather than the text of what was said.
- Appropriations committee pages for the Interior-Environment bill, which is where EPA funding is set.
- News searches such as "Interior-Environment appropriations EPA" or "EPA funding continuing resolution."

# README summary
## GovInfo Scraper

GovInfo Scraper queries the U.S. Government Publishing Office (GovInfo) documented public API to retrieve structured metadata and direct document links for federal documents — including congressional bills, enacted public laws, the daily Congressional Record, committee hearings and reports, the Federal Register, and federal court opinions. For each document it emits a single structured record containing a stable package identifier and collection code, short title (popular title), optional official long title (from the package record), congress and bill metadata parsed from the package identifier (congress number, bill type and number, document version), publication and last-modified dates, issuing bodies, and direct public links to the PDF and full-text HTML. The Actor uses the documented api.govinfo.gov search route (API key supported), follows cursor-based pagination (offset cursor), reads rate-limit headers per response, retries transient server errors with linear backoff, logs per-collection results and failures, and supports optional per-document package-record fetches (extra API requests) to include official abstracts/long titles. It runs without a browser, proxies, or GovInfo account and is designed to support scheduled monitoring and downstream document ingestion pipelines.

## Use cases

- Legislative tracking for policy teams (watch bills and enacted laws; diff on package identifiers between runs)  
- Build a bill-monitoring alert product (keyword-scoped, newest-first monitoring)  
- Legal research corpora (collect federal court opinions, committee hearings, reports, with direct text links for ingest)  
- Scheduled monitoring / automated sweeps of selected GovInfo collections and date ranges  
- Feeding document ingestion pipelines with direct PDF and full-text HTML links and structured metadata

**Short answer: I found no sign that a federal court has blocked the current EPA methane rule.** The sources I could read don't show that any court has stayed, vacated or paused it. My search was limited, so I can't rule out a very recent order.

**What the sources show:**
- **2024 rule:** The D.C. Circuit refused to stay the rule on July 9, 2024. The Supreme Court also denied a stay on Oct. 4, 2024 (*Oklahoma v. EPA*, No. 24A213), with no recorded dissents. The merits case, *Texas v. EPA* (No. 24-1054), was later put on hold in February 2025 while the Trump EPA reconsidered the rule.
- **Rollbacks by the EPA itself:** Harvard's Environmental & Energy Law Program tracker (last updated June 8, 2026) says EPA extended compliance deadlines in 2025. It then issued a final rule on April 6, 2026 that loosens requirements for flares and vent gas.
- **Current litigation:** Environmental groups are challenging the EPA's rollbacks, not defending a court block. EDF filed a petition on June 8, 2026 against the April rule (No. 26-1152, D.C. Cir.). Other environmental groups sued in 2025 over the deadline extensions.
- **Related measures:** Congress used the Congressional Review Act to repeal the methane Waste Emissions Charge rule. The charge itself remains in the statute, and Congress barred EPA from collecting it until 2034.

**Older headlines:** Search results included "Court Blocks E.P.A. Effort to Suspend Obama-Era Methane…" and "Federal Appeals Court Issues Temporary Stay of EPA Rule…". I couldn't open those pages. The first appears to be the 2017 D.C. Circuit decision that vacated EPA's delay of the Obama-era rule. I don't know which rule the second one refers to. I also couldn't read the "Federal court blocks Trump EPA on air pollution" result, so I can't say what it covers.

If you mean a specific recent ruling, tell me the rule or the date. I can look for it directly. For a definitive answer, check the D.C. Circuit docket for No. 26-1152 or the Harvard EELP tracker.

# Supreme Court declines to block EPA methane, mercury rules

![amy-howe thumbnail](/_next/image/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Fpito4za5%2Fproduction%2F05a8a23fd24f6e9a1c433f8483a0820aeda4a2fa-600x601.webp%3Fw%3D2000%26h%3D2000%26fit%3Dcrop%26crop%3Dfocalpoint&w=96&q=75)

By[Amy Howe](https://www.scotusblog.com/author/amy-howe/)

/Oct 4, 2024

![The,United,States,Supreme,Court,Is,Seen,In,Washington,,Dc,](/_next/image/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Fpito4za5%2Fproduction%2F5f7be476092efa7b9f75a9dc70ffab7c0e2e4324-2560x1707.jpg%3Fw%3D2000&w=1920&q=75)

(MattCC716 via Flickr)

The Supreme Court on Friday turned down a request from Republican-led states and industry groups to block a rule from the Environmental Protection Agency that imposes more stringent standards on emissions of hazardous air pollutants from coal-fired power plants. At the same time, the justices turned down a similar request from Oklahoma and industry groups to block an EPA rule that seeks to regulate emissions of methane, a powerful greenhouse gas, from crude-oil and natural gas facilities.

Friday’s orders mean that both rules will remain in effect while challenges to them move forward in a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C.

The orders leaving the EPA rules in place come three months after the Supreme Court put another EPA rule, intended to reduce air pollution that affects air quality in “downwind” states, on hold while challenges to it continue in the lower courts.

The EPA issued the first rule as part of the “Hazardous Air Pollutants” program established by the Clean Air Act, which targets pollutants – such as mercury, arsenic, and nickel – that can be toxic for humans.

The challengers – which include 23 Republican-led states, power plants, mining companies, and industry groups – went to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit seeking review of the rule. They also asked the court of appeals to put the rule on hold while the litigation went forward, but the D.C. Circuit rejected that request. The challengers then came to the Supreme Court in August, filing seven separate applications to stay the rule while the D.C. Circuit’s review continued.

The challengers complained that the new rule will impose billions of dollars in costs on power plants without providing any real public health benefits. Instead, the challengers suggested, the rule is part of a broader plan to (as the states, led by North Dakota contended) “force a nationwide transition away from coal for putative climate change reasons – pursuing a national policy choice this Court has expressly held the agency lacks authority to make.”

The EPA published the methane rule in March. Here too Oklahoma and the industry groups went first to the D.C. Circuit, seeking to challenge the rule and to have that court put it on hold while the litigation continued. The D.C. Circuit denied the request for a stay in July, prompting the challengers to come to the Supreme Court in August.

In brief unsigned orders on Friday, the justices turned down both sets of requests to put the rules on hold. The justices did not provide any explanation for their decisions, and there were no recorded dissents.

The court has not yet acted on a third set of requests to stay a different EPA rule, aimed at reducing emissions of carbon dioxide by power plants. Those requests were filed beginning in late July and have been fully briefed for over a month.

# EPA VOC and Methane Standards for Oil and Gas Facilities

Last updated:

June 8, 2026

Agencies

[EPA](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/agency/epa/)

Actions

Slated for Rollback

![Pipes with valves on water with sun setting int he distance over trees.](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/iStock-1468710968.jpg)

[Current Status](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/tracker/epa-voc-and-methane-standards-for-oil-and-gas-facilities-2/#status) [Why it Matters](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/tracker/epa-voc-and-methane-standards-for-oil-and-gas-facilities-2/#why-it-matters) [Key Resources](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/tracker/epa-voc-and-methane-standards-for-oil-and-gas-facilities-2/#key-resources) [Timeline](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/tracker/epa-voc-and-methane-standards-for-oil-and-gas-facilities-2/#timeline) [Experts](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/tracker/epa-voc-and-methane-standards-for-oil-and-gas-facilities-2/#experts)

## Current Status

In 2024, EPA finalized [three rules](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/methane-rules-for-the-oil-and-gas-sector/) regulating methane from the oil and gas sector: [regulations](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/epas-final-methane-rule-incorporating-advanced-technologies-and-emissions-data-to-reduce-methane-emissions-from-the-oil-and-natural-gas-sector/) for VOCs and methane from the oil and gas sector (NSPS OOOOb/EG OOOOc), [revisions to the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program Subpart W](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-05-14/pdf/2024-08988.pdf), and implementation of the [Waste Emissions Charge](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/final-rule-implementing-the-waste-emissions-charge-for-petroleum-and-natural-gas-systems/) in the Inflation Reduction Act, which has been repealed by the Congressional Review Act. In March 2025, Congress prohibited EPA from collecting the Waste Emissions Charge until 2034. In September, EPA proposed to delay the [Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program Subpart W program](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-09-16/pdf/2025-17923.pdf) until 2034. In November 2025, [EPA finalized the deadline exemptions](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/12/03/2025-21788/oil-and-natural-gas-sector-climate-review-extension-of-deadlines-in-standards-of-performance-for-new) for certain provisions of the NSPS OOOOb/ EG OOOOc rule.

## Why it Matters

Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas released from oil and gas production, processing, transmission, and storage through equipment leaks, venting, and flaring. As technologies advance to better detect and reduce methane emissions and markets develop to demand gas with lower methane emissions, there is an opportunity to design state and federal regulations that align such incentives and ensure methane emission reductions

During the Obama administration, EPA set standards for volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and methane emissions for new oil and natural gas sources (which included production, processing, transmission, and storage). This was the first rule expressly targeting methane emissions. The first Trump administration revoked nearly all of these standards, leaving in place only some of the standards controlling VOCs from new sources. See EELP’s analysis of the first Trump rescissions, [EPA’s Final Methane Emissions Rules Roll Back Standards and Statutory Authority](https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/epas-final-methane-emissions-rule-rolls-back-standards-and-statutory-authority/).

Starting in 2021, the Biden administration and Congress took steps to reinstate and expand the Obama-era methane standards for new and existing oil and natural gas sources. On June 30, 2021, President Biden signed a Congressional Review Act resolution [passed](https://www.congress.gov/bill/117th-congress/senate-joint-resolution/14/actions) by Congress that revoked the Trump administration’s rule. The US also jointly announced a [methane reduction pledge](https://www.globalmethanepledge.org/) with the EU in September 2021, ahead of COP26. Now over 155 countries are participating, with each agreeing to undertake voluntary actions to collectively contribute to reducing global methane emissions by 30 percent from 2020 levels by 2030.

The second Trump administration is taking initial regulatory actions to pause the collection of methane emissions from the oil and natural gas sector, eliminate the legal foundation for regulating greenhouse gas emissions under the Clean Air Act, and reconsider the regulations requiring methane emission reductions.

prompt: What did the Supreme Court decide in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo?
finalAnswer:
I didn't run any Actors. Court-opinion scrapers exist in the Store, but this is a settled, well-documented decision, so I answered from what I know.

**Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (June 28, 2024)**

The Supreme Court ruled 6–3 that courts must use their own independent judgment to decide what a statute means. They may not defer to a federal agency's reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous statute. This overruled ***Chevron U.S.A. v. NRDC* (1984)**, which had required that deference. Chief Justice Roberts wrote the majority opinion. Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson dissented. Justice Jackson did not take part in the companion case from the First Circuit, *Relentless, Inc. v. Department of Commerce*, which was decided together with this one.

**Background:** Herring fishing companies challenged a National Marine Fisheries Service rule. The rule required fishing vessels to pay for the onboard observers who monitor compliance. The agency based this on the Magnuson-Stevens Act. The lower courts upheld the rule under *Chevron* deference.

**Reasoning:**
- **Administrative Procedure Act:** Section 706 directs courts to "decide all relevant questions of law" and interpret statutory provisions. The Court said this makes statutory interpretation a judicial job, not an agency's.
- **Chevron's premise:** The Court rejected the idea that statutory ambiguity means Congress delegated gap-filling power to the agency. It called that presumption a fiction.
- **Delegation still counts:** When Congress explicitly gives an agency discretion, such as by using terms like "appropriate" or "reasonable", courts must respect it. Their job is to police the limits of that delegation.
- **Respect for agency views:** Agency interpretations can still carry persuasive weight under *Skidmore v. Swift & Co.* (1944), based on their thoroughness and consistency. They no longer get binding deference.
- **Precedent:** The Court said earlier cases decided under *Chevron* keep their force under stare decisis. The fact that *Chevron* was later overruled is not by itself a reason to reopen them.

**Significance:** The decision shifts interpretive power from agencies to courts and makes it easier to challenge federal regulations. The dissent argued that agencies have the relevant expertise and that the ruling gives judges policy decisions they are less suited to make.

prompt: When does California's SB 253 climate disclosure law take effect?
finalAnswer:
I didn't run an Actor. This is a legal-timeline question I can answer from what I know, but my information may be out of date.

**SB 253 (the Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act)** applies to U.S. companies that do business in California and have more than $1 billion in annual revenue. Its phases are:

- **Scope 1 and 2 emissions (direct and purchased-energy emissions):** The first reports are due in **2026**, covering fiscal year 2025 data. Under SB 219, which amended the law in 2024, the California Air Resources Board (CARB) sets the exact deadline. CARB's proposed first deadline was **August 10, 2026**.
- **Scope 3 emissions (value-chain emissions):** The first reports are due in **2027**, covering fiscal year 2026 data. CARB is still setting the details.
- **Assurance:** Scope 1 and 2 data need limited assurance starting in 2026. That rises to reasonable assurance in 2030. Scope 3 data need limited assurance starting in 2030.

**SB 261**, the companion climate-risk report law, is a separate statute. Its January 1, 2026 start was put on hold by a court injunction in late 2025. SB 253 was not affected.

The CARB regulations and deadlines were still being finalized and litigated when I last had information. Check CARB's website for the current deadlines before you rely on these dates. I can run a web search to look for the latest status if you'd like.

# README summary
## SEC EDGAR Scraper

A data-extraction Actor that ingests U.S. SEC EDGAR data via the SEC’s official APIs (data.sec.gov, efts.sec.gov, www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar) and emits structured, normalized records for regulatory filings and financial data. Core capabilities include harvesting filing metadata (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, amendments, etc.), extracting raw XBRL facts and normalized financial statements (income, balance sheet, cash flow) mapped to US-GAAP concepts, surfacing full-text search hits across filings, parsing insider transaction reports, exporting institutional (13F) holdings, detecting activist filings (SC 13D/G), and parsing itemized 8-K content. The Actor resolves company identifiers to canonical SEC CIKs, adheres to SEC fair-use rate limits, can produce optional AI-generated filing summaries, and is implemented in TypeScript on the Apify SDK.

## Use cases

- Financial analysts: obtain normalized income statements, balance sheets, and cash flows for U.S. public companies without manual XBRL parsing.  
- Hedge funds & quantitative teams: monitor insider trades, institutional 13F holdings, and activist filings as they are filed.  
- M&A and private equity deal teams: auto-parse 8-K item codes to surface acquisition, executive-change, and auditor-change signals in near real-time.  
- Investment research and AI/LLM teams: ingest multi-year filing archives with structured metadata and optional AI summaries for model training and analysis.  
- Compliance and governance teams: track proxy statements, disclosure trends, and peer filings within date ranges and incremental update runs.  
- Document search and surveillance: full-text search across filings for keyword mentions and regulatory language monitoring.

Supports keyword full-text search across comments, docket-level restriction, date filtering, an option to fetch full bodies (one extra API call per comment), and supplying an API key for higher request throughput; can run with zero configuration to return recent comments. ## Use cases - Government affairs & lobbying: monitor who and what organizations are arguing for or against proposed rules and capture their arguments. - Legal & compliance: read substantive objections to anticipate litigation angles and agency responses. - Policy research & journalism: quantify support vs. opposition, surface mass-comment campaigns, and extract quotable submissions. - Competitive intelligence: track when competitors file comments and what regulatory positions they take. - AI / LLM pipelines: ingest full comment text for summarization, stance detection, entity extraction, or other NLP workflows. # [Input schema](https://apify.com/bikram07/regulations-gov-comments/input) ```json {"title":"Regulations.gov Comments input","type":"object","schemaVersion":1,"properties":{"searchTerm":{"title":"Search term (optional)","description":"Full-text search across comments. # README summary
## Federal Register Search

Searches the U.S. Federal Register via the Government Publishing Office (GPO) API to locate and return structured, machine-readable regulatory records (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents including executive orders) for keyword-driven and filtered queries. The Actor performs full-text keyword matching across titles, abstracts, and document text, applies agency, document-type, date-range, and economic-significance filters, paginates and rate-limits API requests, and transforms nested Federal Register responses into flat, analysis-ready JSON records containing regulatory metadata: primary and all agency names, human-readable CFR references, extracted regulation identifier numbers (RINs), Federal Register citations and signing/publication/effective dates, abstracts, significance flags for Executive Order 12866, and direct HTML/PDF links to official documents; covers the Federal Register archive back to 1994.

## Use cases

- Regulatory compliance monitoring to track new final rules and proposed rules from agencies relevant to a business or sector.  
- Policy research and trend analysis across the Federal Register archive by keyword, agency, and date range.  
- Legal research to locate rules, notices, and presidential documents with structured citation data and CFR references.  
- Lobbying and government affairs monitoring to catch proposed rules during public comment periods.  
- Journalism and investigative reporting focused on executive orders, significant rules, and agency actions.  
- Academic research building structured datasets of regulatory actions for political science, economics, and public policy studies.  
- Building compliance dashboards that track regulatory obligations with CFR references, effective dates, and RIN identifiers.  
- Executive order tracking and aggregation of presidential documents (executive orders, proclamations, memoranda).  
- Multi-agency rulemaking analysis to identify and analyze joint rulemakings involving multiple agencies.  
- Surveillance of economically significant rules by filtering for regulations designated under Executive Order 12866.

# README summary
## eCFR Scraper — US Code of Federal Regulations

Converts the eCFR's XML into clean, section-level JSON records for the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR): one record per CFR section with location metadata (title number and name, chapter, part, subpart, section identifier), heading and legal citation, cleaned full text and discrete paragraph units, and the full hierarchical ancestry from chapter to section. Uses the official eCFR versioner API to fetch snapshots by date and transforms nested regulatory XML into normalized, searchable JSON suitable for text analytics, NLP, full-text search, and downstream retrieval workflows. Supports targeted extraction by chapter/part/subpart and version-dated snapshots to reproduce the CFR as of specified dates, enabling structured outputs optimized for regulatory datasets, semantic search, and RAG pipelines.

## Use cases

- Create legal and compliance datasets from federal regulations at the section level.  
- Monitor regulatory changes and track CFR updates over time using dated snapshots.  
- Feed cleaned section-level texts and hierarchical metadata into RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) and other NLP pipelines.  
- Produce structured inputs for full-text search, indexing, and semantic search over federal regulations.  
- Convert nested eCFR XML into normalized JSON for downstream analysis, citation extraction, and hierarchy-aware processing.

# README summary
## Marine Weather Scraper

A marine forecast extractor that resolves coastal place names or offshore coordinates and converts ocean-model output into structured, export-ready records per location. It extracts significant wave height, wave direction and period, separates swell and wind-wave components (height, direction, period), provides sea-surface temperature and ocean current velocity/direction, and can produce timestamped hourly or daily time series alongside location metadata. The Actor is geared toward generating multi-point marine datasets for surf forecasting, passage planning, fisheries, coastal operations and marine research.

## Use cases

- Surf forecasting: show wave height, period and swell breakdown for individual breaks.  
- Sailing and boating: plan passages using wave and current conditions.  
- Fishing applications: combine sea-surface temperature with wave state for location selection.  
- Coastal operations and port safety: monitor sea state for operations and works.  
- Research and analytics: build multi-point time series of wave, swell, temperature and current metrics.

# README summary
## US Coast Guard Vessel Inspections Scraper

A scraper that extracts structured vessel safety and inspection records from the US Coast Guard's public vessel database: it collects vessel identity (name, IMO/official numbers, call sign, flag, service type, registry status, build year/age), physical dimensions (lengths, breadth, depth, draft in metric and imperial), tonnage metrics (gross, net, deadweight, displacement), certificates with issuing organization and issue/expiry dates, and complete inspection histories including dates, inspection types and outcomes, port/zone, inspector narratives with regulatory references, classified deficiency taxonomy (system/sub-system/component), action codes and resolution status/dates, detention markers, and derived risk metrics (deficiency counts, unresolved items, deficiencies per inspection, days since last inspection, deficiency counts by system, inspection ports). Data is extracted live from public records and returned in a normalized, search- and analysis-ready form suitable for scoring and ranking hull risk.

## Use cases

- Charterer and owner vetting: screening hull detention and deficiency histories before contracting or acceptance.  
- Marine insurance and P&I underwriting: pricing risk using age, class, deficiency density and detention history.  
- Ship finance and sale-and-purchase due diligence: checking condition history and certificate status for valuations.  
- Port and terminal safety screening: flagging inbound vessels with open deficiencies.  
- Classification societies and maritime consultants: benchmarking deficiency patterns by flag, system and vessel type.  
- Maritime research and journalism: tracing substandard shipping, flag-of-convenience patterns and pollution enforcement through inspector narratives and enforcement actions.

# README summary
## Elevation & Terrain Data Scraper

An Apify Actor that returns terrain elevation and ocean depth for arbitrary latitude/longitude points by querying the public OpenTopoData service; it produces per-point records with geographic coordinates, elevation in metres and feet (negative values indicate depth), the digital elevation model (DEM) that supplied the value, a coverage indicator, point ordering, cumulative ground distance for route profiles, source attribution and a timestamp. Technical capabilities include three sampling modes—single-point sampling, bounding-box gridded sampling with configurable spatial resolution, and route/profile sampling that resamples waypoints into evenly spaced ground-distance samples using haversine distances and emits cumulative path distance. The Actor is powered by multiple verified DEMs and bathymetry sources (examples: SRTM, ASTER, Mapzen Terrarium, GEBCO, ETOPO1, Copernicus EU-DEM, USGS NED, BKG DGM, New Zealand LiDAR, EMODnet), returns explicit nulls for locations outside a DEM’s coverage rather than substituting zeros, and implements batching and rate-control against the public OpenTopoData instance to respect upstream request limits. Typical outputs are pointwise elevation profiles, gridded terrain rasters, and DEM identifiers for downstream GIS, modelling and analysis.

## Use cases

- Route and hiking elevation profiles: generate plottable elevation vs. distance profiles from waypoint lists.  
- Solar and wind siting: produce terrain rasters for shading, slope, aspect and wind-exposure modelling.  
- Flood risk modelling: sample elevations across floodplains to compare heights against reference datums and rank locations by elevation.  
- GIS and data pipelines: enrich coordinate tables (properties, towers, plots, delivery stops, sensor sites) with elevation and DEM provenance for analysis.

# README summary ## Chokepoint & Maritime Risk Monitor Daily maritime chokepoint monitoring and risk data: produces per-chokepoint transit counts and trend analytics for 28 global chokepoints (examples: Strait of Hormuz, Bab el‑Mandeb, Suez Canal, Panama, Bosporus, Kerch, Malacca, Taiwan Strait). For each chokepoint it reports latest daily transits and tanker transits, short-term (7‑day) and medium-term (30‑day) averages with year‑over‑year comparisons, a disruption level determined by percent change versus the same window one year earlier (severity tiers), 7‑day breakdowns by ship type (tanker, container, dry bulk, general cargo, ro‑ro) and average carried capacity in tons, plus optional daily history (up to 400 days). It also emits one record per active navigational warning containing NAVAREA/subregion identifiers, message metadata, full warning text, region tags (Persian Gulf/Hormuz, Red Sea/Gulf of Aden, Black Sea/Ukraine, Eastern Mediterranean, Taiwan/South China Sea, Baltic) and risk keywords (missile, firing, drone, GNSS jamming, mine, piracy, etc.). Core data sources and processing: IMF PortWatch transit data derived from AIS ship tracking and NGA Maritime Safety Information (MSI) warnings; calculations include rolling averages, year‑over‑year percentage change, and categorical disruption classification useful for maritime traffic monitoring, trade-flow analysis, and event-driven risk signals. ## Use cases - Commodity and freight traders monitoring chokepoint throughput and tanker activity for market signals - Shipping and insurance risk teams assessing transit disruptions and navigational warnings - Supply‑chain planners tracking chokepoint capacity and short‑term trend changes - Journalists covering regional crises (e.g., Iran/Red Sea, Russia–Ukraine) requiring transit and warning context - AI agents and analytical systems that need structured maritime context (transit counts, trend flags, and safety/warning texts) # [Input schema](https://apify.com/weirworks/chokepoint-maritime-monitor/input) ```json {"title":"Chokepoint & Maritime Risk Monitor","type":"object","schemaVersion":1,"properties":{"include":{"title":"Include","description":"Which datasets to output.","type":"array","default":["chokepoints","warnings"],"items":{"type":"string","enum":["chokepoints","warnings"],"enumTitles":["Chokepoint transits (IMF PortWatch)","Navigational warnings (NGA)"]}},"chokepoints":{"title":"Chokepoints","description":"Names to include (partial match), e.g. Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb, Suez, Bosporus, Kerch. prompt: How do I renew my USCG Merchant Mariner Credential?
finalAnswer:
No Actor in the Apify Store covers this. It's a regulatory how-to question, not a data-extraction task, so I'm answering from general knowledge. Fees and procedures change, so check the current details with the USCG National Maritime Center (NMC) before you submit anything.

## Renewing a USCG Merchant Mariner Credential (MMC)

**1. Check your timing**
- An MMC is valid for 5 years.
- You can submit a renewal up to 8 months before expiration without losing any time on the new credential.
- You can renew after expiration, but you can't legally work in a position that requires the credential until it's renewed.

**2. Gather your documents**
- **Application for Merchant Mariner Credential (CG-719B)**. Check the box for renewal.
- **Proof of sea service or a refresher course**. Typically you need one of these:
  - 1 year (360 days) of sea service within the last 5 years, or
  - 3 months (90 days) of sea service within the last 12 months, or
  - an approved refresher course, or
  - a passing exam score, for some endorsements.
  - Requirements vary by endorsement. For example, STCW endorsements have their own rules.
- **Medical certificate (CG-719K)**. This must be a current one. The medical exam is valid for 2 years from the date it was signed.
- **Drug test result**. You need a negative DOT 5-panel test within the last 6 months, or proof of being in a random testing program in the last 6 months. Note that the Coast Guard may not require this for every renewal.
- **Proof of identity and citizenship**, if you haven't already submitted it. This applies mainly to first-time applications.
- **TWIC**. You must hold a valid TWIC card, and your MMC application generally requires you to have one.
- **Fee payment** through pay.gov. Fees change, so confirm the current amount. A renewal evaluation fee was about $100 in recent years.

**3. Submit your application**
- Submit by email to the NMC (**IACredentialing@uscg.mil**), or by mail or in person at a Regional Exam Center (REC).
- Check the NMC website for the current preferred submission method.

**4. Track your application**
- Use the NMC's Application Status tool or email the NMC.
- Once it's approved, your new credential is mailed to you.

## Tips
- Start early. NMC processing times can run for weeks.
- If you hold STCW endorsements, check that your medical certificate carries the STCW endorsement. Also check whether you need any refresher or revalidation training.
- Your sea service letters should state your vessel, tonnage, days served, and position.

**Official resources:** The NMC page at **www.dco.uscg.mil/nmc** has the current forms, checklists, and fee schedule. You can also call the NMC Customer Service Center at **1-888-427-5662**.

If you tell me your endorsement (for example, OUPV, Master 100 GRT, or Engineer) and your sea service situation, I can help work out which renewal requirements apply to you.

# README summary ## Chokepoint & Maritime Risk Monitor Daily maritime chokepoint monitoring and risk data: produces per-chokepoint transit counts and trend analytics for 28 global chokepoints (examples: Strait of Hormuz, Bab el‑Mandeb, Suez Canal, Panama, Bosporus, Kerch, Malacca, Taiwan Strait). For each chokepoint it reports latest daily transits and tanker transits, short-term (7‑day) and medium-term (30‑day) averages with year‑over‑year comparisons, a disruption level determined by percent change versus the same window one year earlier (severity tiers), 7‑day breakdowns by ship type (tanker, container, dry bulk, general cargo, ro‑ro) and average carried capacity in tons, plus optional daily history (up to 400 days). It also emits one record per active navigational warning containing NAVAREA/subregion identifiers, message metadata, full warning text, region tags (Persian Gulf/Hormuz, Red Sea/Gulf of Aden, Black Sea/Ukraine, Eastern Mediterranean, Taiwan/South China Sea, Baltic) and risk keywords (missile, firing, drone, GNSS jamming, mine, piracy, etc.). Core data sources and processing: IMF PortWatch transit data derived from AIS ship tracking and NGA Maritime Safety Information (MSI) warnings; calculations include rolling averages, year‑over‑year percentage change, and categorical disruption classification useful for maritime traffic monitoring, trade-flow analysis, and event-driven risk signals. ## Use cases - Commodity and freight traders monitoring chokepoint throughput and tanker activity for market signals - Shipping and insurance risk teams assessing transit disruptions and navigational warnings - Supply‑chain planners tracking chokepoint capacity and short‑term trend changes - Journalists covering regional crises (e.g., Iran/Red Sea, Russia–Ukraine) requiring transit and warning context - AI agents and analytical systems that need structured maritime context (transit counts, trend flags, and safety/warning texts) # [Input schema](https://apify.com/weirworks/chokepoint-maritime-monitor/input) ```json {"title":"Chokepoint & Maritime Risk Monitor","type":"object","schemaVersion":1,"properties":{"include":{"title":"Include","description":"Which datasets to output.","type":"array","default":["chokepoints","warnings"],"items":{"type":"string","enum":["chokepoints","warnings"],"enumTitles":["Chokepoint transits (IMF PortWatch)","Navigational warnings (NGA)"]}},"chokepoints":{"title":"Chokepoints","description":"Names to include (partial match), e.g. Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb, Suez, Bosporus, Kerch. Leave empty for all 28.","type":"array"},"onlyDisrupted":{"title":"Only disrupted chokepoints","description":"Only chokepoints whose 7-day transits are 25%+ below the same week last year.","type":"boolean","default":false},"dailyHistoryDays":{"title":"Daily history (days)","description":"Attach this many days of daily transit counts to each chokepoint row.","type":"integer","default":0},"warningRegions":{"title":"Warning regions","description":"Only warnings mentioning these regions. Leave empty for all active warnings.","type":"array","items":{"type":"string","enum":["Strait of Hormuz / Persian Gulf","Red Sea / Gulf of Aden","Black Sea / Ukraine","Eastern Mediterranean","Taiwan Strait / South China Sea","Baltic Sea"]}},"warningKeywords":{"title":"Warning keywords","description":"Only warnings containing any of these words, e.g. MISSILE, GNSS.","type":"array"},"securityWarningsOnly":{"title":"Security-related warnings only","description":"Only warnings mentioning military activity, firing, missiles, drones, mines, GPS/GNSS jamming, piracy or attacks.","type":"boolean","default":false},"proxyConfiguration":{"title":"Proxy","description":"Not needed: public sources.","type":"object","default":{"useApifyProxy":false},"prefill":{"useApifyProxy":false}}}} ```

# README summary
## FAA Drone Airspace Checker

A batch airspace-screening Actor that queries FAA Aeronautical Information Services (AIS) ArcGIS layers to produce a structured, per-coordinate airspace verdict for UAS operations. For each input point it evaluates UAS Facility Map (LAANC) grids, charted Class B/C/D/E surface-area boundaries, prohibited areas, national-defense TFR areas, special-use airspace (Restricted/MOA/Warning/Alert/Danger), part-time National Security UAS Flight Restrictions (NSUFR), stadium proximity, and FAA-listed recreational flying sites; it synthesizes those sources into a categorical verdict about whether FAA airspace authorization is required, the recommended authorization pathway (LAANC auto vs manual FAA DroneZone vs special-use coordination vs prohibited/no authorization required), the LAANC ceiling in feet AGL and controlling facility context, intersecting restriction severity and details, per-layer status/truncation indicators, data provenance (timestamps and map effective date), and an explicit inconclusive/error gating when any queried layer fails. The Actor is optimized for batch work (one row per coordinate) and includes a live drift preflight that validates FAA service names, geometry and canaries before producing results.

## Use cases

- Part 107 remote pilots pre-qualifying job sites to determine LAANC eligibility and authorization pathway before quoting.
- Drone service providers and fleet operations batch-screening scheduled jobs to route crews around authorization bottlenecks.
- Surveying, inspection, roofing, solar and construction teams screening property portfolios for aerial-survey feasibility.
- Drone insurers and risk teams scoring an operating area or reconstructing the airspace context of a claim.
- AI agents and automated workflows chaining a clean, machine-readable airspace screening tool into larger decision processes.
